relations.py:82-165 verify_base_tables handles dialect=="mysql" (lines 97-102, 123-142): it calls connection.cursor(), then cursor.execute/fetchone with %s placeholders (pymysql paramstyle) against information_schema, and cursor.close() in finally. mysql sql_runner.py:125 calls verify_base_tables(conn, args.sql, dialect="mysql") with its pymysql connection. sql_runner.py:155 calls verify_base_tables(conn, args.sql, dialect="postgres") with the psycopg2 connection, after set_session(readonly=True) (line 141) and the optional SET statement_timeout (145-152). relations.py:108-122 handles dialect=="postgres" with a plain read-only SELECT over pg_catalog.pg_class/pg_namespace using pg_catalog.to_regclass(%s) (param-style matches psycopg2). A SELECT is permitted inside a read-only transaction, and to_regclass returns NULL for missing relations, which the code treats as kind None and blocks (fail closed, lines 149-152). Unsupported dialects raise RlsError (line 144). The cursor is closed in finally. The rejection lines about connection: Any are consistent with the head bytes and do not alter this result.

sql_runner.py:94-134. The connection is opened with mode=ro URI plus PRAGMA query_only=ON. An explicit conn.execute("BEGIN") is a deferred transaction, so it is allowed under mode=ro and query_only. The snapshot starts at the first read, which is the catalog check in verify_base_tables (line 134). It is held until commit or close, so cursor.execute at line 136 sees the same schema snapshot. Python's sqlite3 only auto-BEGINs before DML, so the explicit BEGIN does not conflict with it. A failure of BEGIN, such as a nested BEGIN, raises sqlite3.OperationalError, which is a sqlite3.Error. The code catches exactly sqlite3.Error at line 130. It then re-raises as RlsError, which is a deliberate wrap of the caught error and not a different type coming out of BEGIN. No rejections line covers this claim.

sql_runner.py:125-151: BEGIN at 129 is only opened under require_base_tables. Read path returns at 141 and the finally (147-151) closes the connection with no commit, so sqlite3 rolls back the read-only transaction and nothing is left open. Exceptions (RlsError, verify failure, timeout) also reach the same finally and roll back. Non-read path commits at 143, which commits the BEGIN transaction, and then closes. Every exit path is handled. No rejection line covers this subject.

relations.py:135-140 composes `WHERE BINARY {schema} = BINARY {schema_arg} AND BINARY {name} = BINARY {name_arg}`, using the BINARY operator form (not CAST(... AS BINARY)). MySQL documents the BINARY operator as deprecated since 8.0.27 (it still works and only emits a deprecation warning, including in 8.4). So the claim 'non-deprecated SQL on supported MySQL versions' is false. The syntax is valid and the semantics are right: BINARY LOWER(col) = BINARY LOWER(COALESCE(%s, DATABASE())) compares bytes, and folding is applied only when lower_case_table_names != 0 (lines 96-102, 132-134). The rejections lines cover other defects (connection typing, VC-44, exp.Table rebuild) and not this one. The deprecation is cosmetic now, but it will break if the operator is later removed.

relations.py:123-129 lowercases both db and name before matching _METADATA_VIEWS['mysql'], consistent with the comment. An unqualified name gives db '' which is not in the allowlist, so it goes to the catalog lookup. I found no counterexample input. This rests on MySQL server semantics, not on code in the repository.

SQLite pragma_table_list.type takes the values table, view, shadow or virtual. relations.py:43-52 sets the sqlite view kinds to {view} and the base-table kinds to {table}. relations.py:145-152 raises RlsError 'database views are not supported...' for a view, which matches 'view'. For any kind outside both sets (virtual, shadow) it raises 'row-level security could not verify a base table; query blocked', which matches 'base table'. The FTS5 test (test_rls_views.py:228-238) creates a virtual table, so its type is 'virtual', which is not in {table}, so the guard raises the message the test matches. The test skips when FTS5 is not compiled in. I did not run the test. The rejections lines do not cover this claim.

relations.py:43-47 _VIEW_KINDS postgres {'v','m'}, mysql {'VIEW','SYSTEM VIEW'}. pg_catalog.pg_stats is a relkind 'v' view (not in the _METADATA_VIEWS postgres list at lines 26-30, so it is not exempted) and reaches line 145-148, raising RlsError 'database views are not supported...' which contains 'view'. information_schema.COLUMN_STATISTICS is listed in information_schema.TABLES as TABLE_TYPE 'SYSTEM VIEW' on MySQL 8 (from catalog knowledge, not run), and is absent from the allowlist (line 34 lists 'statistics', not 'column_statistics'), so it hits the same message. relations.py:94 connection.cursor() is before the try at 95, so a failure there never reaches finally cursor.close() (153-154). The guard uses its own cursor, so the reuse question does not apply.

The defect was fixed. _accepts_relation_check no longer exists (grep of head src: no matches). It was replaced by _declares_relation_check at src/sqllens/safety/__init__.py:203-217. That function requires a parameter literally named require_base_tables, of kind KEYWORD_ONLY or POSITIONAL_OR_KEYWORD, and its docstring says a bare **kwargs does not count. RlsGuardRunner.__init__ (lines 138-145) raises TypeError for a runner with rules whose run_sql lacks that parameter, so a **kwargs-only runner is rejected at construction. A runner that declares the keyword and ignores it is still undetectable, but that is not the **kwargs hole the finding describes.

The head docstring of src/sqllens/safety/__init__.py:6-23 still says 'Four orthogonal protections' and lists exactly four bullets: read-only, RLS, timeouts, row cap. It says the engine runner verifies on its execution connection that every referenced relation is a base table or an allowlisted metadata-only system view. It also says any other view or unverifiable relation blocks the query. The prior finding said the fail-secure set was described without this check. That is fixed. The count of four matches the bullets, so there is no counting drift.
